extracted.intended_audience: covered entities providing health programs or activities (health care providers, health insurers, State Exchanges and recipients of Federal financial assistance), their legal/compliance staff, accessibility and IT staff, and advocacy organizations
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory standards and requirements under the Department of Health and Human Services' Section 1557 final rule covering effective communication, auxiliary aids and services, facility accessibility, ICT accessibility, reasonable modifications, and nondiscrimination on the basis of sex for health programs and activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of effective communication via qualified interpreters
rubrics_metrics.description: Covered entities are responsible for providing effective communication, including through utilizing the services of a qualified interpreter, and cannot require an individual to bring someone to interpret for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persons with disabilities may bring an interpreter of their choosing, including a family member; OCR declines to add language prohibiting use of family members as interpreters. This approach is consistent with ADA title II regulations (28 CFR 35.160(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patient choice to bring an interpreter (including family members)
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons with disabilities can bring an interpreter of their choosing, including a family member.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covered entities cannot require that an individual bring someone to interpret for them; although OCR recommends using qualified interpreters, it will not forbid a patient's chosen companion from serving as an interpreter except in exigent circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of patient preference for interpreter gender
rubrics_metrics.description: Covered entities should consider a patient's preference for the gender of the interpreter whenever possible, including when requested for religious practices and beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR recommends consideration as a best practice but declines to codify a requirement regarding interpreter gender; whether communication is effective does not inherently depend on satisfying gender preference. Organizations (e.g., NAD) have position statements advising providers to honor gender preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmatively asking and documenting accessibility needs (best practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Providers should 'affirmatively ask' patients what they need to make documents accessible and document that requirement so needs do not have to be repeatedly asked and answered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR recognizes this as a best practice (example: Medicare beneficiary default accessible format process) and encourages covered entities to implement such documentation in written effective communication procedures under §92.8(e), but declines to mandate documentation in the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance documents are advisory (not codified regulatory requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: OCR guidance, technical assistance, and enforcement materials advise the public how the agency understands its legal authorities but are not codified into the regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR declines to incorporate referenced guidance and enforcement materials directly into the final rule because these materials evolve; they remain useful as advisory resources for covered entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auxiliary aids and services must be provided free of charge
rubrics_metrics.description: Auxiliary aids and services must be provided free of charge to individuals with disabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR revised §92.202(b) to state explicitly that auxiliary aids and services must be provided free of charge, consistent with ADA title II and title III approaches that forbid surcharges on persons with disabilities (see 28 CFR 35.130(f), 36.301(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Auxiliary aids and services: accessible formats, timely, and protect privacy/independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Auxiliary aids and services must be provided in accessible formats, in a timely manner, and in such a way as to protect the privacy and independence of the individual with a disability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR revised §92.202(b) (consistent with 28 CFR 35.160(b)(1)) to clarify these elements so readers can immediately identify the free/timely/privacy/independence requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auxiliary aids and services: non-exhaustive examples and broad scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The examples of auxiliary aids and services in §92.4 are non-exhaustive; covered entities may use additional aids and services to achieve effective communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR explicitly recognizes that entities may need to provide other tools, including plain language materials and screen reader capabilities, and may tailor auxiliary aids to the individual's needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) devices and supports
rubrics_metrics.description: AAC devices and related equipment, acquisition or modification of devices, and training and assistance in their use can be required auxiliary aids and services to ensure effective communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include speech-generating devices, single-message devices, computers, tablets, smartphones, amplification devices, telecommunications devices, voice amplifiers, artificial phonation devices, picture and symbol boards, paper-based aids, and other compensatory equipment. Training on device use is often necessary to ensure effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different communication strategies for cognitive/neurological/psychiatric disabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective communication for patients with cognitive, neurological, or psychiatric disabilities may require auxiliary aids/services or strategies different from those used for other disabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: an individual with cognitive disability may require additional time with the provider and plain language answers rather than an ASL interpreter; covered entities must tailor approaches to the nature of the disability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of effectiveness for communication (not 'reasonable attempt')
rubrics_metrics.description: Covered entities must ensure communications with people with disabilities are as effective as communications with others; the rule does not change the standard to require only a 'reasonable attempt.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fundamental alteration or undue burden defenses remain available per 28 CFR 35.164 and section 504 standards, but the baseline obligation is parity of effectiveness, not mere reasonable efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undue burden and fundamental alteration defenses apply per existing law
rubrics_metrics.description: If compliance would result in a fundamental alteration in the nature of the program or an undue financial/administrative burden, a covered entity may invoke those defenses as defined under section 504 and ADA regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule adopts existing standards (e.g., 28 CFR 35.150(a)(3), 35.164, 35.130(b)(7)); DOJ guidance and technical assistance materials provide additional context on these defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facility accessibility: comply with 2010 ADA Standards for new construction/alterations
rubrics_metrics.description: New construction or alteration of buildings or facilities must comply with the 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR will continue to retain the requirement that new construction/alterations follow the 2010 Standards. UFAS is not allowed as the accessibility standard for new facilities; UFAS is used only to determine compliance for buildings built before July 18, 2016 in certain circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program accessibility (viewed in entirety) vs. per-facility requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Covered entities must operate programs and activities so that, when viewed in their entirety, they are readily accessible to individuals with disabilities; neither the ADA nor section 504 requires each existing facility to be made accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program accessibility obligations apply to existing facilities as well as new construction and alterations; coverage overlaps with other statutes and implementing regs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical and Diagnostic Equipment (MDE) accessibility under consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: OCR notes commenters' requests to incorporate U.S. Access Board 2017 Standards for MDE and will continue to address accessible MDE in related rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR referenced a separate NPRM proposing adoption of Access Board's 2017 MDE standards for recipients of Federal financial assistance (proposed 45 CFR 84.92).

rubrics_metrics.name: ICT accessibility obligation for covered entities (§92.204)
rubrics_metrics.description: Covered entities must ensure that their health programs and activities provided through ICT (including websites and mobile applications) are accessible to individuals with disabilities, unless doing so would result in undue financial/administrative burdens or a fundamental alteration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a required action would cause such burdens or alterations, covered entities must take other actions that do not cause those burdens but still enable, to the maximum extent possible, access to programs and activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: ICT procurement and vendor responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Regardless of procurement method, covered entities are obligated to ensure that the ICT they procure, design, maintain, or use to provide health programs and activities is accessible to individuals with disabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covered entities remain responsible for the accessibility of third-party provided ICT even if third-party vendors are not directly covered by the regulation; commenters suggested use of VPAT/Section 508 documentation to evaluate vendors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mobile applications are included as ICT
rubrics_metrics.description: Mobile applications used to provide health programs and activities are expressly included under §92.204(b) and must be accessible for individuals with disabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Privacy concerns related to certain mobile apps (e.g., SUD treatment) are outside the scope of this rulemaking, but HIPAA guidance on mobile health apps exists; OCR encourages awareness of privacy interplay.

rubrics_metrics.name: No adoption of specific accessibility standard or safe harbor at this time
rubrics_metrics.description: OCR decided not to adopt specific accessibility standards (e.g., WCAG, section 508) or a safe harbor deeming compliance with a standard as compliance with §92.204 at this time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR encourages covered entities to incorporate current WCAG standards as they take steps to comply; OCR and DOJ have parallel NPRMs proposing standards for other statutory programs, and OCR may coordinate with those efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance timelines, size-based differentiation, and exemptions (commenter suggestions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters proposed varied compliance timelines (60 days to 2 years), phased approaches prioritizing critical telehealth fields, and small business exemptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR did not adopt specific timelines or small business exemptions in this rule; OCR will provide technical assistance and educational materials but cannot provide financial assistance to ensure ICT accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarification on undue burden/fundamental alteration for ICT
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests for further guidance on what constitutes undue burden or fundamental alteration were noted; OCR relies on existing ADA/section 504 standards and DOJ technical assistance/manuals for context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule does not create a different standard for undue burden/fundamental alteration; DOJ's ADA NPRM and technical materials offer familiar standards and further context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable modifications to policies, practices, or procedures (§92.205)
rubrics_metrics.description: Covered entities must make reasonable modifications to policies, practices, or procedures when necessary to avoid discrimination on the basis of disability, unless the modification would fundamentally alter the nature of the service, program, or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation follows 28 CFR 35.130(b)(7). A covered entity is not required to provide a reasonable modification to an individual who meets the 'regarded as' prong of the definition of disability at §35.108(a)(1)(iii). Determinations of fundamental alteration are fact-specific; OCR declined to enumerate exhaustive examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal program access on the basis of sex (§92.206) — general obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: Covered entities must provide individuals equal access to health programs and activities without discrimination on the basis of sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §92.206(a) establishes the general prohibition; enumerated examples in (b) amplify types of discriminatory actions that are prohibited but do not limit the general prohibition in (a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal program access on basis of sex (§92.206) — specific prohibitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibitions include: (1) denying or limiting health services (including those offered exclusively to individuals of one sex) based on sex assigned at birth, gender identity, or gender otherwise recorded; (2) denying or limiting a health care professional's ability to provide services on that basis; (3) applying policies that separate/treat individuals differently that cause more than de minimis harm; (4) denying or limiting gender-affirming care when denial is based on sex assigned at birth or gender identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §92.206(c) clarifies nothing in the section requires provision of any health service where there is a legitimate nondiscriminatory reason (e.g., clinical appropriateness). The enumerations in (b) do not limit the general prohibition in (a). Matters related to reproductive health and fertility are addressed in §92.208.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referral to other sections for specific topics (e.g., reproductive health, MDE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific topics referenced by commenters (e.g., reproductive health care, fertility treatments, MDE standards) are addressed in other sections of the rulemaking (e.g., §92.208 for reproductive health) or in separate rulemakings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR refers commenters to those sections or separate proceedings for detail rather than expanding §92.206 or other provisions beyond their scoped content.
